Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to follow in debate the leading speaker for our party, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) who, with characteristic modesty, a modesty which has become his hallmark, did not indicate to the House that it was during the government of my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in which he was the minister of trade and commerce, that the program of which he spoke was started. He laid a cornerstone, I think, in a modern era of Canadian government, dedicated to the assistance of small business.
I spoke to the minister before the dinner break this evening and I told him 1 thought this was an excellent bill, and that the time had long since passed when the government ought to forget its passion for large business and large corporate enterprise and give some constructive thought to the problems of small business in Canada.
Although it hasn't been said before in this debate, and it does not take away in any way from the goodness of the bill before the House tonight, the problems felt by small business are due in no small way to the attitude of the government toward small business.
You have only to speak to small businessmen; they will tell you they have felt discriminated against by government. They feel the government looks upon small business with indifference, and they have reason to feel that way. They feel there is excessive regard given by governments generally, and by the present government in particular, to the supposed virtues of large size. They claim that the government is overly concerned with large firms, not because of their real contribution to the national wealth- and they do make a contribution-but because of a mistaken equation of great size with great efficiency. I think hon. members know that this equation does not necessarily apply. I want to repeat to the minister that I do not in any way detract from the qualities of the bill reforms,

which I look upon as constituting a new beginning for small business.
Small business is indeed in trouble in certain areas of Canada. It is fighting a rearguard action in the economic sphere. In 1962, for instance, a 10.4 per cent share of the nation's income went to small business. In 1973, the share had fallen to 7.5 per cent, and I dare say when the statistics are viewed for 1974 we shall see a further fall off in terms of the share of the national income to small business.
Small businesses are a unique form of enterprise. They provide a productive outlet for the energies of Canadians who are enterprising people and who want to be independent in terms of their economic way of life. I believe they exhibit a greater efficiency when stacked, pound for pound, against large business. They have a capacity to become the specialist suppliers of large business and they add variety and service, a specialized skill, to the economic life of our country.
They provide competition. It cannot be over-emphasized that they do constitute a bulwark against monopoly in business, and they provide the means for the entry into productive business of many young people. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings mentioned the number of people who are employed in small businesses. They employ half the people in Canada. They are a large and developing source of employment. They provide for new directions and new methods of doing business, and they offer an opportunity for personal initiative which, in a society such as ours, is growing less and less.
I commend the minister for recognizing these things even though that recognition has come somewhat late. My experience with the Industrial Development Bank was as a solicitor, acting for people who applied to the bank for capital. I found that the greatest complaint among those of my clients who made application-and this was fairly general-was the lack of flexibility in the attitude of the bank toward the difficulties of small business. I do not suggest the officials were actively pursuing this policy. They were prudent, cautious, bankers.
Like the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings I hope experience will show that the movement of the bank out of the banking atmosphere and into the atmosphere of industry, trade and commerce will provide an expansionist viewpoint for the first time toward small business in terms of financial assistance.
I hope the minister can undertake, when he closes this debate, that the attitude of this bank when it functions will not be to stack against the number of loans the small numbers of business failures. Rather, I hope the bank will deal with this from the point of view of the amount of loans, because sometimes viewing it from the small amount of business failures among businesses which have been backed by the bank it may indicate an attitude of too great conservatism and not enough adventure by the government in the application of this fiscal agent to those whom I regard as some of the greatest adventurers, in the economic sense, that there are, namely, the small businessmen in this country. If there is to be an emphasis at all on the flow of capital from the bank to aid business, it ought to be in that direction. I hope this will be considered in the

committee and that the minister and the officials of the bank will consider it as well.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to speak on Bill C-14 this evening. This bill has the potential to help business expansion in Canada, and especially small businesses which I feel are the backbone of the nation.
The objects of the new Federal Business Development Bank are to promote and assist in the establishment and development of business enterprises in Canada through financial assistance, management counselling and training. With business failures totalling 1,412 for the first quarter of 1974 in Canada, it will be hoped that the development bank's management and counselling training will slow down the number of business bankruptcies.
A section of the bill which I favour is the appointing of regional advisory councils which will have a better understanding of Canada's regional needs than a centralized advisory group in Ottawa. Many aspects of the bill are similar to the Canadian investment credit incentives program which was introduced by the Conservative party in October, 1972. We in the Conservative party realized then that, with the fantastic amount of business failures in Canada, immediate and decisive action must be taken to assist small business in Canada.
Attempts at tax reform led the federal government to ignore the vital interests of small business, and yet small business in this country generates more employment, more real growth, more tax revenue, and bears more of the cost burden of government than does the so-called big business.
Full employment is a national priority, and for this we must look to those elements in our economy which are less influenced by technological change and that remain labour-intensive, such as small business. Far too much of this section of our economy is presently ignored and excluded from consideration by government policy, and excluded from the encouragement of fiscal incentives. Bill C-14 should encourage these incentives.
Assistance, financial and otherwise, unfortunately is not the only answer to help business grow in Canada. Commercial enterprises in Canada, large and small, are experiencing great difficulties in finding workers, both
Federal Business Development Bank Act skilled and unskilled. Yet we have thousands on welfare and on the Unemployment Insurance Commission rolls, and we also have to import workers to help keep some industries going. Strange but true. Recently two motels had to close down in Banff because they could not find help. Until the work ethic is restored in Canada, financial assistance alone to business will not be sufficient to keep it going or expanding.
The introduction of the just society and the leisure society since 1968 has brought about this deterioration of the work ethic in Canada. The blame for worker shortage, while thousands are collecting unemployment insurance, lies squarely upon the Liberal government and its mismanagement of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I would like to quote from a letter I have just received from the executive vice-president of the Winnipeg Builders Exchange as an example of the difficulties they have in finding manpower. They also point out how workers play games with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I quote:
Three months from now our industry will again be entering that difficult stage where we are unable to obtain skilled manpower to work on our projects during the winter-a time of the year when large numbers of skilled tradesmen have been laid off due to the seasonal swings in the construction industry.
This situation has worsened each of the past winters until it reached the point during January, 1974, where our association took an active role in the employment scene. We detailed completely the requests of employers for more than 100 tradesmen of varying qualifications; followed the applications made to both the union hiring centres and Canada Manpower offices; followed up weekly and in some cases semi-weekly for the placement of these people; and followed bi-weekly with the employers to determine the results they were receiving. The employers, on their part, kept detailed records of every person applying to them or sent to them for work, including names and addresses. We were then able to report to the Unemployment Insurance Commission the number who refused to work in their trade in jobs requiring their comparable skills.
One of the results of this activity by our office-aside from the main objective of securing employees for our members-was that we were able to establish beyond any doubt in our minds that jobs were going vacant while skilled tradesmen qualified to fill those jobs refused to work and were drawing unemployment insurance benefits. Keep in mind that we are not discussing unskilled labour, but rather skilled tradesmen able to demand and receive the equally high rates of pay they later find it convenient to accept when summer arrives.
Last winter, we had openings for carpenters within 50 miles of the city, but candidates forwarded by Canada Manpower refused the jobs when they found that they were outside city limits. We have shortages in several other trades as well, and only in the fields of the electricians and plumbers were we able to fill our needs.
There can be no doubt that one of the greatest flaws in the current unemployment insurance regulations is the one which allows renewal of unemployment insurance benefits, or establishment of benefits, in a period of eight weeks. It is hard to imagine a philosophy that has hurt the national economy more in recent years than that voiced publicly by a former cabinet minister to the effect that people have a right not to work. That philosophy haunts industry even today, and has both increased costs and reduced productivity-both effects being large factors in the inflationary spiral which we experience in Canada today.
While there are many aspects of the unemployment insurance regulations which we feel need revision, one of the most significant is that there should be an extension of the qualification period for benefits to a minimum of 20 weeks rather than the eight weeks under the current regulations.
This is just one example of what business people are experiencing across Canada, and immediate corrective

October 17, 1974

In closing, Mr. Speaker, while we in the Conservative party support Bill C-14, it is not the complete answer for assistance to business in Canada. The government also has a responsibility to restore the work ethic in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-14 and to express support for what I think is an outstanding bill, in view of some of the tremendous merits it envisions for small industries and small businesses. The government should be justly proud of the Federal Business Development Bank. This bill will help Canadians to extend their imaginations well into the market place. It is a bill with a particular emphasis on small business and developments, and is an attempt to act into law a philosophy that is long overdue.
This is a philosophy which says to every Canadian: "You are someone who counts; you are someone who matters". This philosophy says to the Canadian people: "Go ahead and dream, and the government will give support". I find it very easy to lend support to this bill because it is a bill that is steeped in Conservative thinking. It is the kind of thing which says that the individual matters. It is the kind of thing which places the individual in the forefront as he should be.
This is a sharp demarkation and departure from the traditional system of taxing people so that the government can think up and execute its ideas. I might submit that execution is what usually comes from dreams by big government under its own implementation. This is a great bill because the people of Canada become the thinkers and doers, and the government does what it must do. They all play a supportive role. This bill challenges people to seek the maximums of their potential. That situation is as it should be.
While I wholeheartedly support this bill I wish to take a few moments to outline a caution, to which I think we should lend particular attention. I say this with all due awareness that there is a regional advisory system or council set up to help administer this bill. The special concern I suggest is that we must be very attentive to the sparsely populated areas of this country. I would hope there is special concern not only for small business but for the sparsely populated areas.
In the first century of Canada's federated existence its rural and urban population ratios have completely reversed. One hundred years ago 80 per cent of Canadians lived in rural areas. Today over 80 per cent of Canadians live in urban areas. It is predicted that 95 per cent of all Canadians will be living in urban centres by the year 2000. If there is something that is obvious it is that government must bear the brunt of the responsibility for the fact that a large proportion of this country's population has been crammed and crowded into a few large cities.
Past policies of the two highest levels of government have had a tremendous influence on the rural exodus. To lend documentation to that, I point out that in the single decade from 1961 to 1971 over 179,000 people left the rural

communities on the prairies. That means that in only ten years almost 200,000 people have vanished from those areas. I request that through this bill there be a real thrust to decentralize Canada. This means special help for the rural communities. They have, however, a serious handicap.
In some of the major cities of the country there are whole office staffs set up to assist the cities in obtaining assistance from the provincial and federal governments. The small towns throughout the country do not have that kind of staff. They operate with part-time mayors who hold other jobs. The way in which they can make application for and attract small businesses does not have such a degree of sophistication, and so I believe it becomes important that very special attention be paid to the small and rural communities.
A few years ago we heard the slogan that the land is strong. In the context that that slogan was used its real meaning was that people are strong. But I submit that there cannot be a concept of a strong land that is devoid of people. All across the prairies we see a mass exodus of people from the rural districts. The land is not strong if it does not have people. Small businesses and industries in those areas must have the kind of thrust that is extra-projected within the scope of this legislation.
We cannot afford to continue to lose 200,000 people within a single decade from the rural areas. That simply is too many. It is well for those who have driven across the prairies to note the number of dying towns. The fact remains that how they were set up caused them to be placed too closely together. Largely they were established under the historical notion that towns were far enough apart if one could load a sleigh with grain, drive into town in the middle of winter and be back home again before dark. That placed them at something like six to nine miles apart.
We who have seen these towns die know it is not a death that came about through suicide, or lack of desire, or lack of spirit on the part of the people in them. It is instead murder by technology and a murder by government which through its policies, caused the development of this country to be centralized in five major locations or five major cities. We must pay special attention to rural communities throughout the breadth and scope of this country.
There is a myth which exists in western culture that bigness is goodness. It is the kind of myth which we must do everything we can to end. If we take a look at the large cities in this North American continent we will note that almost everything associated with bigness, in terms of the size of cities, tends also to perpetuate negative behaviour. There are many things which exist in such a society which cause people to go to institutions because of negative behaviour. The growing ratio in this regard is faster than the growth in the size of the cities.
Rural people, of course, are no better than city people. I submit, however, they are just as good. The rural way of life is something which must be protected and not allowed to vanish from the Canadian scene. If the land is to be strong it must be a land from sea to sea, which means people from sea to sea, which means support for growth and industrial development all across the country. Canada cannot be allowed to go along as a malignant growth
October 17, 1974

which clusters together like a cancer choking into one or two small areas all the development that this country is planning.
So, Mr. Speaker, I applaud the government for this bill. I think it has the kind of potential which can do a great deal to encourage the thrust of the individual and to encourage small business development all across the country. But I ask that particular attention be paid to the fact that in the smaller communities the assistance of government will be needed even in terms of helping to make applications to this bank, and much work is needed in those small communities.

speechtext:
I hope that the new Federal Business Development Bank will serve the purposes for which it is intended, but for the life of me I cannot see how it will do anything more for the small businessman than the many other programs which already exist under other departments of government, other than build another little empire to add to the bureaucracy and confuse further the potential businessman to whom it is supposedly directed, not to mention the added cost to the taxpayer in setting it up.
The Federal Business Development Bank is not much different from the present Industrial Development Bank other than the few fancy frills such as are contained in clause 21 wherein it provides management assistance to recipients of loans, and it is empowered under clause 22(b) to sponsor conferences, seminars and the like, and under clause 23 to distribute information relating to techniques, methods and practices for the successful administration of business enterprises.
Furthermore, this type of assistance is being offered under various other programs in federal and federal/pro-vincial programs. An example of the duplication, Mr. Speaker, is that in most provinces in Canada there are many provincial development corporations, such as the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation, which serve almost the exact same purposes. Of the $22 million in capital funds, $20 million has been invested by the federal government under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.

Here are the objectives of the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation. I have already circulated a pamphlet to all hon. members setting these out. In order to overcome the lack of detailed information concerning viable opportunities for investment, lack of venture capital, and the failure of businesses to meet the demands for more sophistication in their approach to business development, a positive program for the development of small and medium-sized businesses was drawn up in 1973 to provide businesses with industrial intelligence; management advisory services; project information; loan financing for the establishment, expansion or modernization of programs; equity financing, and related services and assistance.
The corporation's affairs are governed by a board of directors with strong business backgrounds and knowledge of the particular economy, which works closely with the federal government. The main emphasis will be on financial assistance and management advisory services. However, there is vast scope for expanding activities and consequently there will be ongoing development work.
Then, Mr. Speaker, it designates the financial assistance available, term loans, and application requirements. We are all aware that most of our provinces have similar programs to suit their requirements.
Now, let us look at this new Federal Business Development Bank. Its objectives*are almost the same-to provide financial assistance, management training, information and advice and other such ancillary services in order to promote and assist in the establishment of businesses in Canada, with authority to set up regional advisory boards to suit the particular region. Both of these agencies have the same objectives worded in a different manner.
Despite the various other loan programs such as the Small Business Loans, Fisheries and Farm Improvement Loans, Farm Syndicate Loans, Vessel Building Loans, Small Farm Development Loans, Capital Assistance Loans, Rural Development Loans, and besides the government guaranteed loans under DREE and the various agencies to assist the small businessman under the minister's department-such as CASE-there remains that vacuum which the minister and his advisers cannot recognize. That vacuum is the need to provide venture capital to small business.
The need is not to build another bureaucracy under another department, Mr. Speaker. All that will do is further confuse the small businessman. There will be more confusing and lengthy application forms to fill out, and all he will receive, as happens in most cases, is a form letter advising him that he does not qualify, without giving any reason.
Setting up a dozen more fancy corporations will not help. The need is to overcome the discouraging high interest rates, the excessive requirements for collateral, the lack of risk capital, the constant desire that seems to exist in the bureaucracy to refuse an applicant and get rid of a problem rather than to help him.
Going back for a moment to the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation, this agency loaned out almost $5 million in its first year of operation. Along with other programs many millions have been injected, but even with this injection of funds Newfoundland still
October 17, 1974

has an embarrassing 16 per cent unemployment rate in a population of only a little over a half million.
Over the years that I have been in this House I have taken the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to task for the lack of responsibility shown by the chartered banks of Canada with regard to small business loans, fisheries improvement loans and farm improvement loans. In reply to the concern which I expressed in the House I received the following letter from the minister, dated May 6, 1974:
You will recollect that during the debate on second reading of Bill C-14, an Act to Amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, Small Businesses Loans Act and Fisheries Improvement Loans Act-you pointed out that far fewer loans under these plans were going to the province of Newfoundland than to any of the other provinces of Canada. In response I undertook to have Mr. Claude Passy-
He is the chairman of the guaranteed loans administration, Mr. Speaker.
-investigate the points you raised on the spot in St. John's.
And this is what happens, Mr. Speaker. They go to the capitals and do not care about the other parts of the provinces where the development potential exists. The letter continues:
Mr. Passy advises that, after discussion with the senior official of one of the banks in Newfoundland, the following points were made:
1.	The policy of the banks in Newfoundland is to participate in these plans.
2.	In so far as the official's bank was concerned all applications for these loans made in the province were accepted and processed.
3.	Small Businesses Loans. There are not a great number of small businesses in Newfoundland and, traditionally, such businesses have obtained all their credit needs through a commercial institution- largely the chartered banks. Banks continue to meet the needs and hence there are very few applications for or questions about the small business loans. It is only recently, within the last two-three years that the economy in Newfoundland has taken an upturn and it is expected that this may result in more demand for credit. In this connection you will be aware that the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation was set up in 1973 to stimulate new industry and the development of small businesses.
As I indicated already, Mr. Speaker, the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation does the very things that this new Federal Development Bank is going to try to do. Sometimes I wonder if most of the ministers in the government just say to themselves, "Program, program, who has the best program?" They all want a loan program in order to build an empire and see what they can do with Canada, but that is missing the point.
I will not go into more detail on this, Mr. Speaker, because I know some of my colleagues want to speak. The letter goes on to talk about farm improvement loans and fisheries improvement loans, but what it says is happening just is not happening, Mr. Speaker.
I say that the chartered banks, under the guaranteed loans provisions, just do not care about their responsibility; it is greater than just making as much profit as possible. They even go to the point of discouraging government guaranteed loans because, if the applicant is a good risk, they can give him a conventional loan and charge a higher rate of interest.
No, Madam Speaker, I repeat, the answer is not in forming new corporations under new departments of government which will compete with one another. The
Federal Business Development Bank Act answer is not in spending more millions of necessary dollars to take over a similar agency which is fulfilling the same purpose. I say the answer is to amalgamate the various cumbersome programs now in existence and which are going off in the same direction through different avenues, and to recognize the initiative and knowledge of the Canadian who understands resource potential. Let us support his initiative with the capital he needs and with a little more faith and understanding as to our aims in building more small businesses, if we believe they are the backbone of our economy.
I think the government should either amalgamate existing programs, and there are many, or review them with the common sense purpose of expanding their requirement standards, so that we can meet the need of the small businessman, whether he be a farmer, fisherman, hotel keeper, sawmill operator or small manufacturer. I say that the only way we can expand small business is to ease the restrictions which exist and provide more venture capital to the prospective entrepreneur. In this way we will provide the opportunity which is lacking and, thereby, the job opportunities we need in Canada if we are to overcome unemployment and build a better nation.

Mr. Speaker, I am in general agreement with the thrust of the bill and feel that it may help some small business operations. I am inclined to think that the establishment of a federal bank for this purpose will be valuable.
From my observations over six years the operations of the IDB in my constituency have not been successful. I have become skeptical of the manner in which these loans are funded and placed. I find that there are fewer applications for loans than was originally anticipated when the legislation was brought down. Perhaps such legislation does not function well in a western rural riding like mine. Yet the IDB has been the only vehicle by which some businessmen in my riding have been given the chance to obtain federal government backed loans. Legislation of that type just does not function too well in certain areas, for reasons which may be inherent in the administration of this type of financing.
I have found, Madam Speaker, that the IDB has been hopeless in supplying the needs of my riding. The reason seems to be that service and similar industries have a very low priority with the IDB, which interests itself in industry and industrial projects. There are few industrial projects in my riding. I have found that because our projects are small, personnel often do not have the background of business experience, expertise and credit rating which the IDB seems to want.
Nearly always applicants for loans are beaten before they start because the officers of IDB always ask for a performance record which cannot be met. Often the individual has not been in manufacturing before. In my experience, once a business is started it can get along with capital generated locally. But the starting of these industries is the problem.
Indeed, there is considerable reluctance to expand any industry or business beyond what the individual or a family can handle, because of the great difficulty in disposing of a business at the end of the individual's working

October 17, 1974
Adjournment Debate
career. I have found that many relatively successful businessmen have been put in a position in which their businesses have become too large to sell. They cannot find buyers to take their businesses off their hands.
In other words, under our present economic climate a small business is usually regarded as a living only for its owner. I believe we shall see more of this attitude in future. That means that businesses will tend to remain small or disappear on the death or retirement of the owners.
This bill will be applied differently in the different areas of Canada. I think we are aware of the marked regional differences in this country. We have spent much time asking what is a small business. I have found, in discussions with members who represent constituencies in Ontario and Quebec, the central part of Canada, that a small business is looked on as one with 40 or 50 employees. In my part of the world a small business supports four or five employees at most.
The IDB, in conformity with the terms under which it operated, was not interested in small loans of up to $10,000 or $15,000, which small businessmen often needed. The IDB wanted to lend them a good, big chunk of money, $50,000 or more. I often thought the officers of IDB felt that a $10,000 loan was not contributing much, or was too small to be of value. I have found that civil servants often judge the success of their work by the size of transaction they handle.
If this bill can overcome some of the old administrative difficulties, it will become a valuable tool for helping small businesses. May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-DOWNSVIEW AIR BASE-POSSIBILITY OF RELEASING LAND FOR HOUSING DEVELOPMENT
NATIONAL DEFENCE-DOWNSVIEW AIR BASE-POSSIBILITY OF RELEASING LAND FOR HOUSING DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to talk this evening in general terms about the future of Downsview Airport, which is in North York in the municipality of metropolitan Toronto. This area includes an important military distribution centre, a military airport and an aircraft frame factory and testing area which once was a wholly owned subsidiary of a British corporation. Now all these lands, over 1,000 acres, are owned by the federal government, and the use of the land has not changed for at least two decades.

During these past two decades the greatest possible change of use has taken place in the lands surrounding this area. Farm land and waste land have been converted and become one of the world's fastest growing cities, the municipality of North York.
Governments and citizens tend to be critical of slum landlords and absentee landlords, on the ground that they lose touch with local standards and local needs. I say that in relation to Downsview, and other lands which the federal government owns in the municipality of metropolitan Toronto, the federal government itself is a slum landlord and an absentee landlord. In proof I wish to make two points.
Compare the way the federal government uses its land in Ottawa with the way it uses the excess land at Downsview air base. It had a lot of land in the Ottawa area that was surplus and unused. What happened? An agency was established, the NCC. This agency has established bicycle paths and amenities for the surrounding communities. It has, much to its credit, innovatively established a system of allotment gardens so that people who are stuck in apartments can rent unused plots of land to grow flowers and vegetables. All this takes place in the shadow of Parliament Hill under the watchful eye of the minister.
What is being done 250 miles away in Toronto with unused parts of Downsview Airport? Absolutely nothing. The vacant parts have laid in that condition for years.
As a second proof I wish to point out that back in 1970 the Department of National Defence itself recognized that there were 70 acres of land that were not required. It turned that land over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation to be put to some better use. We can think of a lot better use for that land in that area than simply lying vacant.
Four years ago two other government departments put a hold on that land. What happened to it? Absolutely nothing. It has just remained unused in the middle of a residential area where housing is badly needed.
Two important changes have taken place in the past few months which I hope will make a difference to the federal government. First, the aircraft plant has been taken over by the federal government. For the first time the federal government controls the destiny of the entire holding.
Second, a subway station and subway line are in the process of being built on the edge of this land. Imagine, people who live in Orangeville are travelling to Toronto to work. Their transportation involves three hours a day, back and forth, while their government has much of 1,000 acres of land vacant, and there will be a subway station right at the corner.
It is time the federal government asked itself whether this is the right place for an airport and a factory. I do not think it is. It is time to conform to what the local community requires and is doing. I do not have a comprehensive list of changes that ought to be made, but I wish to make a number of points.
First, there should continue to be a strong military presence in the area. The distribution centre is important. It needs to be manned. That use in that area is entirely
October 17, 1974

justified. There is military housing surrounding it. That housing should be continued for that purpose. In fact, more housing should be built in that area for military personnel who very often have short-term duty there and cannot find alternative accommodation.
Second, a lot of attention should be given to the need for amenities and community facilities in that area because in some parts of the surrounding territory the municipality gave inadequate thought to the needs of the residents. This is a good way to make a contribution toward improving those communities.
Third, vast parking areas will have to be established there so that people can come to the subway station, park their cars and get into the city. Parking facilities will be required.
Fourth, this is an obvious place for a lot of housing, hopefully partly for veterans and military personnel. In addition, there is room for sensible, attractive low density and mixed density residential use. This is something that is badly required in the area. I could add that if the Veterans Land Act is terminated next March, it will be a measure of justice to the military of Canada and veterans that some provisions are made for them in this area.
Fifth, I wish to draw attention to the interest of some groups in metropolitan Toronto in establishing in that area the United Nations university campus. I think that is a fine idea. I would like to know a lot more before I agree with it, but I would note that one of the most attractive features of that proposal is they do not intend to put up a lot of new buildings. They recognize it will be near a subway station. Additions to the university will take advantage of empty buildings, and available buildings are located throughout Metropolitan Toronto.

Local interests add up to regional interests and are perfectly deserving of expression on the floor of the House. I also note his reference to the fact that the military presence is of importance to the area.
Adjournment Debate
The department has received repeated requests over several years to give up the Downsview site. In 1970, after considerable pressure from the Borough of North York, 69 acres were declared surplus and turned over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. This parcel of land is the only part of the site considered suitable for housing development. However, the property has not been disposed of by the Department of Public Works, presumably because agreement for disposal by the Treasury Board Advisory Committee on federal land management is still awaited.
There is a continued requirement for Downsview by the Department of National Defence, and no plans are in offing to declare any other parts of the site surplus. However, as the hon. member said, negotiations for an exchange of property in the southwest corner are in progress between National Defence Headquarters and the regional municipality of Toronto to permit a right-of-way for a proposed subway and, at the same time, straighten out a jagged property boundary currently in existence. About four acres of land are involved.
Canadian Forces Base, Toronto, an Air Transport Command Base, is an example of a base which exists mainly for the support of units from other commands, notably the Naval Reserves (Maritime Command Units) and the Militia Air reserve squadrons. It is estimated that at least 50 per cent of the base effort is devoted to the support of the Naval Reserves, Militia units and Air Reserve Squadrons.
With regard to the Downsview site it is anticipated that there will be a continuing requirement for a base to support these reserves and cadets in the greater Toronto-Hamilton areas.
The department has a long-standing agreement with De Havilland Aircraft Corporation for the continuing use of the airfield. Until such time as there is a change in role or function of that firm, a requirement for the lengthy runways will continue.
